title: Pembrolizumab + carboplatin + fluorouracil
context_label: First-line treatment of metastatic or unresectable recurrent head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in adults with tumour PD-L1 CPS ≥1.
indication_text: First-line treatment of metastatic or unresectable recurrent head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in adults with tumour PD-L1 CPS ≥1.
purpose: Pembrolizumab and chemotherapy aim to control head and neck cancer that has spread or returned and cannot be removed. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for you.
schedule_label: Every 3 weeks; up to 6 combination cycles, then pembrolizumab alone.
schedule_summary: Every 21 days: pembrolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1; fluorouracil over Days 1–4. Up to 6 combination cycles, then pembrolizumab alone while appropriate. Every dose depends on safety and benefit review.
administration_text: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is infused over 30 minutes, followed by carboplatin AUC 5 over 30 minutes on Day 1. Fluorouracil is prescribed as 1,000 mg/m² each day by 22-hour infusion on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 48 hours twice. Staff confirm pump changes and disconnection from the actual connection time.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver function, glucose and thyroid tests; hepatitis B surface antigen/core antibody and hepatitis C; tumour PD-L1 CPS and DPD assessment before fluorouracil. Review previous immune problems, transplants, medicines and infection. An isotope GFR measurement is preferred when assessing kidney function for carboplatin dosing; further kidney testing is arranged when indicated. Audiology is considered when indicated. Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose each cycle; thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks and sooner if symptoms require. Ask about bowel, breathing, skin, hormone and other immune symptoms before every dose. A normal blood test does not exclude immune toxicity. Continue reporting possible immune effects after the last dose. Follow unresolved blood, kidney, hearing, nerve or endocrine problems and any prescribed steroid taper or hormone replacement. The team sets disease assessment scans and follow-up; this protocol does not mandate a universal imaging interval or routine blood tumour-marker schedule.

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1, a signal that can limit the activity of immune cells. This can help them attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it ends.
agents.watch: Report new diarrhoea, cough, breathlessness, rash, headache, unusual weakness, thirst or changes in urine promptly.
risks: Immune inflammation of bowel, lungs, liver or kidneys
Thyroid, pituitary, adrenal or glucose problems
Rare heart, muscle, nerve and eye inflammation
Some immune effects need long-term treatment

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.mechanism: Disrupts production of DNA and RNA
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the materials cells need to make DNA and RNA. A pump gives it over the prescribed days. DPD is an enzyme that helps break it down; testing before treatment reduces risk but cannot prevent every severe reaction.
agents.watch: Report severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Rare severe neurological or early excessive toxicity

phases.label: Combination treatment
phases.detail: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is infused over 30 minutes, followed by carboplatin AUC 5 over 30 minutes on Day 1. Fluorouracil is prescribed as 1,000 mg/m² each day by 22-hour infusion on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 48 hours twice. Staff confirm pump changes and disconnection from the actual connection time. The planned combination limit is six cycles; toxicity may change the plan earlier.

phases.label: Pembrolizumab alone
phases.detail: Pembrolizumab 200 mg over 30 minutes every 21 days continues after the combination phase when appropriate, until progression or unacceptable toxicity under this regimen. A six-cycle chemotherapy record is not a six-cycle total course; the protocol does not impose an automatic 24-month stop.

phases_note: Dates and treatment decisions come from your team. A delayed or omitted dose does not count as treatment received.

day_groups.body: No planned chemotherapy after completion of the pump in this reference cycle. Pembrolizumab immune effects can occur at any time.
day_groups.action: Report symptoms early and arrange the next required tests.

urgent_extra: Call the oncology team promptly for fever, sudden illness, diarrhoea, painful mouth, reduced drinking, new breathlessness or immune symptoms. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil needs urgent assessment. Severe chest pain, breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency. Early severe fluorouracil symptoms can occur despite DPD testing.

Four daily 22-hour infusions or two 48-hour infusions may be prescribed. Confirm all change and disconnection appointments.
After the Day 1 infusions, staff start the prescribed pump. Do not calculate or alter its rate.
Daily pump changes or a change after the first 48-hour infusion are arranged by the unit. Protect the line and report leaks or unexpected progress.
Timing is based on actual connection and infusion duration. Keep the appointment; do not disconnect or dispose of the pump yourself.
The access device may stay in place. Follow its dressing, flushing and infection precautions, including during maintenance if it remains.

anatomy: Report severe headache, visual change, unusual weakness, thirst, dizziness or frequent urination.
Report ulcers, painful swallowing or difficulty drinking; early severe symptoms need urgent review.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment; severe breathing difficulty is an emergency.
Chest pain, palpitations, collapse or marked muscle weakness needs urgent assessment.
Blood tests may show inflammation first. Report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or unusual itching.
Report reduced urine, swelling, persistent vomiting or difficulty drinking; kidney results also guide platinum treatment.
Call early for diarrhoea, blood or mucus, pain or dehydration. Different causes need different treatment.
Report rash, painful palms or soles. Blistering, peeling or rash with fever needs urgent assessment.
Report new tingling, weakness, unsteadiness or trouble swallowing. Sudden weakness or speech difficulty is an emergency.
Fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding needs prompt oncology advice.

support.title: One written medicine plan
support.text: Ask for one schedule showing prevention medicines, rescue treatment and what to do if symptoms persist. Do not add, double or restart medicines from an old prescription.

support.title: Immune effects and maintenance
support.text: Pembrolizumab can cause inflammation in healthy organs even after chemotherapy has finished. Keep the alert card and report new symptoms promptly. Steroids or hormone replacement may be needed for specific complications; do not start or stop them without the treating team.

support.title: Food, fluids and weight
support.text: A dietitian can tailor food texture, supplements and calorie or protein needs. Tell the team early if eating or drinking becomes difficult; do not wait for substantial weight loss. Fluid targets depend on kidney and heart health.

support.title: Oral and dental care
support.text: Use the mouth-care plan provided by the team and tell them about ulcers, thrush, bleeding or pain. Inform your dentist about cancer treatment. Before any dental procedure, confirm timing with the oncology team.

support.title: Swallowing and communication
support.text: A speech and language therapist can assess swallowing and advise exercises or safer food and drink textures. Follow the individual assessment; a general guide cannot decide which textures are safe for you.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and medicines
support.text: Discuss fertility and pregnancy precautions before treatment and the medicine-specific duration of contraception afterwards. Ask about breastfeeding. Bring a full medicine, supplement and allergy list; check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.

sections.title: Before the first visit
sections.text: Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and actual urgent contact numbers. Bring any hearing concerns, swallowing problems and medicine list.

sections.title: Time in the unit
sections.text: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is infused over 30 minutes, followed by carboplatin AUC 5 over 30 minutes on Day 1. Fluorouracil is prescribed as 1,000 mg/m² each day by 22-hour infusion on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 48 hours twice. Staff confirm pump changes and disconnection from the actual connection time.

sections.title: Pump visits and line care
sections.text: Record every pump change and disconnection appointment. Device problems need the unit’s instructions; do not reconnect, adjust or remove the line yourself.

sections.title: Practical help
sections.text: Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.

sections.title: Leaving the unit
sections.text: Check the next visit and blood-test dates, support medicines and who to call if unwell. Have the team replace example phone numbers before using the wallet card.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis
chapters.intro: Keep your pathology and agreed treatment goal with your records.

items.title: Site, type and stage
items.text: Ask which part of the head or neck the cancer started in, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and your health affect the options. HPV/p16 testing is relevant to some sites; it is not the same test as PD-L1.

items.title: Which pathway applies?
items.text: First-line treatment of metastatic or unresectable recurrent head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in adults with tumour PD-L1 CPS ≥1. This guide should match the named treatment on your prescription.

items.title: What tumour tests mean
items.text: PD-L1 CPS is used to select this pembrolizumab combination; DPD testing assesses fluorouracil safety. Neither is a general blood tumour marker that measures response.

chapters.title: Treatment choices and your priorities
chapters.intro: The consent conversation explains the boundaries of the plan.

items.title: Benefit and alternatives
items.text: Pembrolizumab and chemotherapy aim to control head and neck cancer that has spread or returned and cannot be removed. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for you. Ask how alternatives compare for your health, goals and previous treatment. A study result cannot predict an individual outcome.

items.title: A pause is a treatment decision
items.text: The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results or your priorities. Record which component is affected and what is needed before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.

items.title: Combining treatment approaches
items.text: This regimen is systemic treatment. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role for an individual symptom or disease plan; concurrent radiation is not automatically part of this combination.

chapters.title: Preparing for and receiving treatment
chapters.intro: Plan the appointments and support around the prescribed schedule.

items.title: Your first visit
items.text: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is infused over 30 minutes, followed by carboplatin AUC 5 over 30 minutes on Day 1. Fluorouracil is prescribed as 1,000 mg/m² each day by 22-hour infusion on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 48 hours twice. Staff confirm pump changes and disconnection from the actual connection time.

items.title: If an appointment changes
items.text: Contact the unit for revised dates after a missed or delayed visit. A missed appointment is not a completed dose. Ask whether blood tests, premedicines or pump appointments also need to change.

items.title: What the record shows
items.text: Write the actual treatment date, phase and any change. The wallet card is a brief record; the passport holds the fuller history. It does not replace the hospital treatment record.

items.title: Your pump and line
items.text: Ask staff to demonstrate the specific device, check progress and explain spill or emergency steps. Call for leakage, damage, disconnection, unexpected completion or a pump that seems not to run. Do not change settings, disconnect or reconnect it yourself.

chapters.title: Between visits: symptoms and medicines
chapters.intro: Use the agreed home plan and contact pathway.

items.title: Symptoms have no fixed calendar
items.text: Some effects appear soon after treatment and others build over weeks. Immune effects may begin during maintenance or after the last pembrolizumab dose. Do not wait for the next appointment if a symptom is new, severe or worsening.

items.title: A medicine plan you can use
items.text: Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines clearly separated on one written list. Record what you have taken and the response, so the team can adjust it. Do not double a missed dose unless your prescriber tells you to.

items.title: When self-care is not enough
items.text: Call the oncology team promptly for fever, sudden illness, diarrhoea, painful mouth, reduced drinking, new breathlessness or immune symptoms. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil needs urgent assessment. Severe chest pain, breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency. Early severe fluorouracil symptoms can occur despite DPD testing.

chapters.title: Mouth, teeth and jaw care
chapters.intro: Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Arrange dental assessment and oral care with the team. If radiotherapy is planned separately, the dental and radiation teams decide any necessary treatment and healing time before it starts.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

items.title: If you have had head and neck radiation
items.text: Earlier head and neck radiation can affect saliva, teeth and healing long afterwards. Tell any dentist about it before invasive treatment. If you have not had radiation, follow the oral-care advice appropriate to your current treatment.

chapters.title: Eating, drinking and maintaining strength
chapters.intro: The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.

items.title: Recognising an intake problem
items.text: Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

items.title: If ordinary food is not enough
items.text: The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.

items.title: Fluid needs are individual
items.text: Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.

items.title: Diarrhoea needs the correct response
items.text: Fluorouracil and pembrolizumab can both cause diarrhoea through different mechanisms. Contact the team early rather than assuming it is ordinary chemotherapy diarrhoea; use rescue medicine only under the written plan.

chapters.title: Swallowing, voice and communication
chapters.intro: A speech and language therapist can help protect function.

items.title: Swallowing assessment
items.text: Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.

items.title: Exercises and rehabilitation
items.text: Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.

items.title: Communication needs
items.text: Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.

chapters.title: Daily life and emotional support
chapters.intro: Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.

items.title: Smoking and alcohol
items.text: Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

items.title: Emotional and practical concerns
items.text: Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.

chapters.title: Recovery, assessment and longer-term care
chapters.intro: Treatment completion and recovery are different milestones.

items.title: Continuing symptoms
items.text: Continue reporting possible immune effects after the last dose. Follow unresolved blood, kidney, hearing, nerve or endocrine problems and any prescribed steroid taper or hormone replacement. The team sets disease assessment scans and follow-up; this protocol does not mandate a universal imaging interval or routine blood tumour-marker schedule.

items.title: Cancer assessment
items.text: Your team sets examinations and imaging around the disease, treatment and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who explains the result. An unbooked scan is not automatically due at a fixed week because a general guide says so.

items.title: Information for other clinicians
items.text: Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, ongoing medicines and relevant alert card. Tell clinicians about earlier immune treatment or head and neck radiation even after the course has ended.

chapters.title: Your records and additional help
chapters.intro: Keep essential instructions available on paper.

items.title: The passport and wallet card
items.text: The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

items.title: Contacts before patient use
items.text: The phone numbers printed as examples must be replaced and checked by the treating service. Add the unit’s daytime, out-of-hours and backup route; keep this information where you and a support person can find it.

items.title: If you prefer paper
items.text: Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: KEYNOTE-048 studied first-line treatment for recurrent or metastatic squamous head and neck cancer.
evidence.population: Untreated locally incurable recurrent or metastatic HNSCC; study analyses included different PD-L1 CPS groups.
evidence.comparison: Pembrolizumab plus a platinum and fluorouracil versus cetuximab plus a platinum and fluorouracil.
evidence.interpretation: The original 2019 report supported pembrolizumab with platinum and fluorouracil in this setting. The chemotherapy group included cisplatin or carboplatin; it does not provide a separate randomised survival estimate for this specific platinum choice.
limitations: The current NCCP indication requires PD-L1 CPS ≥1; a trial’s total population is not a replacement eligibility rule.
The trial was not a direct comparison of carboplatin with cisplatin.
Trial treatment duration does not impose an automatic duration cap absent from the current NCCP regimen.
Group outcomes do not predict an individual outcome.

consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, alternatives and uncertainty; serious or lasting harms; treatment burden; fertility and pregnancy precautions; and the patient’s priorities. Explain low blood counts/infection, bleeding, nausea, mucositis, diarrhoea, fluorouracil cardiac and early severe toxicity, platinum kidney/hearing/nerve effects, DPD testing limits, pump/line complications and immune organ inflammation including permanent hormone replacement. Separate the up-to-six-cycle combination phase from ongoing pembrolizumab maintenance. Confirm actual urgent contacts and teach-back; this draft does not authorise treatment.
